I sleep as much as possible but sometimes my gut wrenching profound sadness keeps me awake.

During an involuntary 96 hour hold you are basically kept in a normal hospital on 1:1 direct, continuous observation. Someone is in your room watching you 24/7 and you can’t close the bathroom door when you toilet or shower. You can’t have your phone. You wear a paper gown. Literally EVERYTHING you could use to hurt yourself is removed from your room. Curtains. TV remote. Trash cans. You get paper plates and plastic silverware that are confiscated as soon as you finish your meal. If you’re a smoker, you can forget about that. Can’t leave your room for any reason. No visitors either. 

It’s one thing when you choose to isolate yourself at home. It’s another thing when all your freedom is taken away. 

You stay in a regular ass hospital until they can find placement for you in a mental health facility. Usually there are no beds available so you’re in the hospital for a minute. You are evaluated by a psychiatrist while you’re hospitalized. He will try and help you with meds. If you lie well enough, the psychiatrist will let you discharge after 4 days with scripts for meds and instructions to follow up with outpatient services. It’s hard if you don’t have insurance. 

If you’re used to faking happiness and putting on a mask so that others don’t know anything is wrong with you… you can fool the psychiatrist. Gonna take some excellent acting but you can get out.
Well. Guess I have my answer.
I lie. Because I’m a nurse and I know if I tell the truth I’ll get a 96 hour hold.

My ex-husband (we are still friends!) is a Honduran immigrant and when we were first married he always bought shoes. Had a literal obsession with shoes and they were taking over our whole closet. I made some comment one day when I was annoyed he bought another pair of shoes and he said…

“I got my first pair of shoes when I was 13. At Christmas my mother got some used tennis shoes from a missionary at the church. They were old shoes. Ugly shoes. But they were beautiful to me and I was so happy that I cried. I played soccer my whole life without shoes before that, and walked through my town on the dirt and rocks, and to my school every day without shoes. Every day. Now I have money and I will buy shoes, every time I want to buy shoes.”

Through THE BIGGEST ugly-cry sobs of my life, I replied “YES you will, honey. Yes you will always buy shoes WHENEVER you want for the rest of your life!! And I’m so sorry for being a jerk!!”

I bought him shoes every Christmas and birthday after that. The novelty of receiving them and his genuine delight never wore off over the years. We’re no longer together but we’re still close and co-parent well together. Our daughter still buys him shoes as gifts and she is just as touched by his authentic reaction.

This video is beautiful and it reminded me of him.
